questions.q: Which branch of pharmacology studies the biochemical and physiological effects of drugs and their mechanisms of action on the body?
questions.explain: Pharmacodynamics deals with what the drug does to the body, including receptor interactions and physiological effects. Pharmacokinetics describes what the body does to the drug.

open.q: Name the branch of pharmacology that studies the biochemical and physiological effects of drugs and their mechanisms of action on the body.

questions.q: Which discipline focuses on the absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion of drugs over time?
questions.explain: Pharmacokinetics quantifies the movement of a drug into, through, and out of the body (ADME). Posology specifically refers to the study of drug dosages.

open.q: Which branch of pharmacology describes the absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion of drugs?

questions.q: What is the specific branch of pharmacology concerned with the determination of appropriate drug dosages?
questions.explain: Posology is the study of drug doses and dosing regimens based on age, weight, and clinical condition. Pharmacognosy is the study of drugs derived from natural sources.

open.q: State the pharmacological term for the study of drug dosages.

questions.q: Which field involves the identification, extraction, and standardization of crude drugs obtained from natural plant and animal sources?
questions.explain: Pharmacognosy investigates medicinal substances obtained from plants, animals, and minerals. Pharmacovigilance monitors adverse drug reactions after marketing.

open.q: Name the branch of pharmacology that deals with crude drugs obtained from natural plant and animal sources.

questions.q: What term describes the science and activities relating to the detection, assessment, understanding, and prevention of adverse drug effects?
questions.explain: Pharmacovigilance monitors drug safety in clinical practice to identify rare or long-term adverse reactions. Toxicology focuses broadly on harmful effects of chemicals and poisons.

open.q: What is the name of the discipline dedicated to detecting, assessing, and preventing adverse effects of medicines?

questions.q: Which term refers to the use of chemical agents to selectively destroy invading pathogens or malignant cells without harming host tissues?
questions.explain: Chemotherapy applies to antimicrobial, antiparasitic, and anticancer agents designed for selective toxicity against foreign or malignant cells.

open.q: Name the therapeutic use of chemical agents to selectively destroy pathogenic organisms or cancer cells in the host.

questions.q: How is a drug formally defined by the World Health Organization?
options: Any chemical agent that cures an infectious disease
A synthetic compound prescribed exclusively by physicians
Any substance used to modify physiological systems or pathological states for the benefit of the recipient
Any alkaloid extracted from medicinal plants for therapeutic trials
questions.explain: The WHO defines a drug broadly as any substance or product used or intended to be used to modify or explore physiological systems or pathological states for the benefit of the recipient.

open.q: State the World Health Organization definition of a drug.
accept: any substance used to modify or explore physiological systems or pathological states for the benefit of the recipient
substance used to diagnose prevent or treat disease

questions.q: Which branch of pharmacology investigates inherited variations in drug-metabolizing enzymes and receptors that alter individual drug responses?
questions.explain: Pharmacogenetics examines single-gene variations (such as G6PD deficiency or slow acetylation) affecting drug response, whereas pharmacogenomics looks at the entire genome.

open.q: Which branch of pharmacology studies how inherited genetic variations affect an individual's response to drugs?

questions.q: Which chemical class of plant-derived drugs consists of basic nitrogenous compounds that react with acids to form water-soluble salts?
questions.explain: Alkaloids (such as morphine, atropine, and quinine) are nitrogen-containing organic bases whose names typically end in -ine. Glycosides contain a sugar moiety linked to an aglycone.

open.q: Name the group of basic nitrogenous organic compounds obtained from plants that form water-soluble salts with acids.

questions.q: From which plant source is the cardiotonic glycoside digoxin obtained?
questions.explain: Digoxin is extracted from the leaves of Digitalis lanata (white foxglove), whereas digitoxin is obtained from Digitalis purpurea.

open.q: Name the botanical plant source from which digoxin is extracted.

questions.q: Which antimalarial alkaloid is derived from the bark of the Cinchona tree?
questions.explain: Quinine and quinidine are alkaloids isolated from Cinchona bark. Artemisinin comes from Artemisia annua, while chloroquine is synthetic.

open.q: Identify the antimalarial alkaloid obtained from the bark of the Cinchona tree.

questions.q: Which plant yields the potent analgesic alkaloid morphine from its unripe seed capsules?
questions.explain: Opium latex from Papaver somniferum (opium poppy) contains phenanthrene alkaloids like morphine and codeine, as well as benzylisoquinoline alkaloids like papaverine.

open.q: State the botanical name of the opium poppy from which morphine is isolated.

questions.q: Atropine is an anticholinergic alkaloid naturally extracted from which plant?
questions.explain: Atropine and hyoscine are tropane alkaloids found in Atropa belladonna (deadly nightshade) and Datura stramonium.

open.q: Name the plant source from which the anticholinergic drug atropine is obtained.

questions.q: Which chemical component of a glycoside is responsible for its specific pharmacological activity?
questions.explain: A glycoside consists of a sugar moiety (glycone) that influences solubility and pharmacokinetics, linked to a non-sugar moiety (aglycone or genin) that exerts the pharmacological effect.

open.q: Name the non-sugar part of a glycoside molecule that determines its pharmacological activity.

questions.q: Which plant-derived antimalarial sesquiterpene lactone is extracted from sweet wormwood (Artemisia annua)?
questions.explain: Artemisinin (qinghaosu) is extracted from Artemisia annua and serves as the parent compound for semisynthetic derivatives like artesunate and artemether.

open.q: Name the antimalarial compound isolated from the herb Artemisia annua.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a mineral source used clinically as a mood stabilizer in bipolar disorder?
questions.explain: Lithium carbonate is a mineral salt used in bipolar affective disorder. Magnesium sulfate is used in eclampsia, ferrous sulfate in iron-deficiency anaemia, and aluminium hydroxide as an antacid.

open.q: Identify the mineral salt used in clinical pharmacology for the prophylaxis and treatment of bipolar disorder.

questions.q: From which microbial organism was the first penicillin antibiotic originally isolated?
questions.explain: Alexander Fleming isolated penicillin from the fungus Penicillium notatum (later Penicillium chrysogenum for mass production). Streptomyces griseus is the source of streptomycin.

open.q: Name the fungal species from which penicillin was first discovered.

questions.q: Which anticoagulant drug is traditionally extracted from porcine intestinal mucosa or bovine lung?
questions.explain: Unfractionated heparin is a naturally occurring glycosaminoglycan sourced from animal tissues (porcine intestinal mucosa or bovine lung), whereas warfarin is synthetic.

open.q: Name the injectable anticoagulant obtained from porcine intestinal mucosa or bovine lung.

questions.q: How are semisynthetic drugs such as amoxicillin and ampicillin produced?
options: Complete chemical synthesis from simple inorganic precursors
Direct extraction from dried leaves without chemical alteration
Chemical modification of a naturally occurring core molecule
Insertion of human genes into bacterial plasmids
questions.explain: Semisynthetic drugs are made by chemically modifying a natural nucleus (such as 6-aminopenicillanic acid) to improve acid stability, spectrum, or pharmacokinetics.

open.q: Define a semisynthetic drug in terms of how it is manufactured.
accept: chemical modification of a natural compound

questions.q: Human insulin and erythropoietin used in modern therapeutics are primarily produced by which method?
options: Extraction from cadaveric human pituitary glands
questions.explain: Recombinant DNA technology expresses human genes in bacteria (like E. coli) or mammalian cells (like CHO cells) to produce pure human insulin, erythropoietin, and monoclonal antibodies.

open.q: Which biotechnological method is used to manufacture modern human insulin and recombinant erythropoietin?

questions.q: Why has recombinant human insulin largely replaced bovine and porcine insulins in clinical practice?
options: It eliminates immunogenicity and species-specific antibody formation
It resists gastric acid degradation and can be taken orally
It has a half-life of several weeks after a single injection
It does not require cold-chain storage at any temperature
questions.explain: Bovine insulin differs from human insulin by 3 amino acids and porcine by 1 amino acid, triggering anti-insulin antibodies and lipodystrophy; recombinant human insulin matches the human sequence.

open.q: Explain the main immunological advantage of recombinant human insulin over bovine or porcine insulin.
accept: identical amino acid sequence to human insulin

questions.q: Which type of drug name is universally accepted, non-proprietary, and assigned by bodies such as the WHO (INN)?
questions.explain: The generic (non-proprietary) name, such as paracetamol or amoxicillin, is standardized globally by the WHO International Nonproprietary Name (INN) system.

open.q: What type of drug name is standardized globally as an International Nonproprietary Name (INN) by the WHO?

questions.q: Why are medical students and clinicians taught to prescribe drugs using their generic names rather than proprietary brand names?
options: Brand names are illegal to write on hospital prescriptions in Nigeria
Generic drugs always contain higher active doses than branded drugs
It prevents dispensing errors from look-alike brand names and lowers patient cost
Generic names describe the exact IUPAC molecular bonding structure
questions.explain: Generic prescribing reduces confusion across multiple trade names for the same active ingredient, enables pharmacist substitution, and reduces out-of-pocket expenditure.

open.q: Give two clinical or economic reasons for prescribing drugs by their generic names rather than brand names.
accept: avoids look-alike brand confusion and lowers expense

questions.q: Into which broad category are oral, sublingual, and rectal drug administration classified?
questions.explain: Enteral routes deliver drugs via the gastrointestinal tract (oral, sublingual/buccal, and rectal), whereas parenteral routes bypass the GI tract.

open.q: Name the broad category of drug administration that includes oral, sublingual, and rectal routes.

questions.q: Which route of administration is the most common, safest, and most convenient for self-administration of systemic drugs?
questions.explain: The oral route (per os) is non-invasive, economical, sterile preparation is unnecessary, and it is suitable for most chronic therapies.

open.q: Identify the safest, most convenient, and most widely used route for systemic drug administration.

questions.q: Why must insulin and benzylpenicillin NOT be administered via the oral route?
options: They cause immediate pyloric sphincter spasm
They are destroyed by gastric acid and digestive proteolytic enzymes
They bind irreversibly to dietary calcium in the duodenum
They are absorbed too rapidly and cause acute toxicity
questions.explain: Insulin is a peptide hydrolyzed by pepsin and trypsin, while benzylpenicillin (penicillin G) is acid-labile and destroyed by gastric hydrochloric acid.

open.q: Explain why peptide drugs like insulin and acid-labile drugs like benzylpenicillin are ineffective when taken orally.
accept: destroyed by gastric acid and digestive enzymes
degraded in the stomach and gut

questions.q: What is the primary pharmacokinetic advantage of administering glyceryl trinitrate (nitroglycerin) sublingually during an acute attack of angina pectoris?
options: It provides sustained release over 24 hours
It undergoes rapid activation by salivary amylase
It bypasses hepatic first-pass metabolism for rapid onset of action
It avoids systemic absorption and acts locally on oral mucosa
questions.explain: Sublingual veins drain directly into the superior vena cava rather than the portal vein, bypassing extensive hepatic first-pass inactivation of glyceryl trinitrate and giving relief within 1 to 3 minutes.

open.q: Explain why glyceryl trinitrate is given sublingually rather than swallowed for acute angina.
accept: direct entry into systemic circulation via superior vena cava

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of a drug administered via the rectal suppository route bypasses the hepatic portal circulation?
questions.explain: The superior rectal vein drains into the portal vein (liver), whereas the middle and inferior rectal veins drain into the internal iliac vein (systemic circulation), so roughly 50% bypasses first-pass metabolism.

open.q: State the approximate percentage of a rectally administered drug that bypasses hepatic first-pass metabolism.

questions.q: A 4-year-old child is brought to the emergency unit in status epilepticus, and intravenous access cannot be established immediately. Which alternative route is best suited for rapid systemic delivery of diazepam?
questions.explain: Rectal diazepam solution or gel is rapidly absorbed through the rectal mucosa and is a standard emergency rescue route in convulsing children when IV access is delayed.

open.q: In a convulsing child where IV access is unavailable, which route is used to administer emergency diazepam?

questions.q: Which parenteral route provides 100% bioavailability and the most rapid onset of systemic drug action?
questions.explain: Intravenous injection places the entire dose directly into the bloodstream without an absorption phase, yielding 100% bioavailability and immediate onset.

open.q: Name the route of administration that achieves 100% bioavailability with no absorption phase.

questions.q: Why must oily solutions and insoluble suspensions NEVER be administered via the intravenous route?
options: They are immediately excreted unchanged by the kidneys
They induce severe hepatic enzyme induction
They can cause fatal embolism and haemolysis
They fail to cross the blood-brain barrier
questions.explain: Oily vehicles or particulate suspensions injected intravenously can obstruct pulmonary or cerebral capillaries, causing fatal fat or particulate embolism.

open.q: State the major life-threatening complication of injecting oily solutions or suspensions intravenously.

questions.q: Which parenteral route allows the safe injection of mild irritants, aqueous suspensions, and oily depot preparations due to rich skeletal muscle vascularity?
questions.explain: Skeletal muscle has richer blood supply and fewer pain fibers than subcutaneous tissue, permitting injection of larger volumes (up to 5 mL), mild irritants, and oily depot formulations.

open.q: Name the parenteral route suitable for administering oily depot preparations and mild irritants due to high vascularity and fewer sensory nerve endings.

questions.q: Which muscle site is preferred in adults for deep intramuscular injections to avoid injury to the sciatic nerve?
options: Upper outer quadrant of the gluteus maximus
Lower inner quadrant of the gluteus maximus
questions.explain: Injecting into the upper outer quadrant of the buttock (or ventrogluteal site) avoids the sciatic nerve and superior gluteal vessels.

open.q: Which anatomical quadrant of the gluteal region is used for intramuscular injections to avoid damaging the sciatic nerve?

questions.q: Which injection site is recommended for intramuscular vaccinations in infants under 1 year of age?
questions.explain: The vastus lateralis in the anterolateral thigh is well developed in infants and avoids the poorly developed gluteal mass and nearby sciatic nerve.

open.q: Name the preferred anatomical site for intramuscular injections in infants.

questions.q: Why should irritating drugs NOT be injected via the subcutaneous route?
options: Subcutaneous fat degrades all water-soluble drugs instantly
Subcutaneous capillaries drain directly into the portal vein
Subcutaneous tissue has rich sensory innervation and poor vascularity, risking severe pain and tissue sloughing
Subcutaneous injections cause immediate systemic anaphylaxis
questions.explain: Subcutaneous tissue has abundant pain receptors and slower blood flow than muscle; irritants cause severe pain, sterile abscesses, or necrosis.

open.q: Explain why irritating substances are contraindicated for subcutaneous injection.
accept: causes severe pain and tissue necrosis
rich sensory nerves and lower vascularity cause sloughing

questions.q: Which parenteral route involves injecting a small volume (0.1 mL) into the layers of the skin, typically for BCG vaccination or tuberculin skin testing?
questions.explain: Intradermal injection raises a small bleb in the dermis and is used for BCG vaccine, Mantoux (tuberculin) testing, and allergen sensitivity testing.

open.q: Name the route of administration used to raise a small skin bleb for BCG vaccination and the Mantoux test.

questions.q: Into which anatomical space is a drug injected during intrathecal administration?
questions.explain: Intrathecal injection delivers drugs directly into the cerebrospinal fluid within the subarachnoid space, bypassing the blood-brain barrier.

open.q: Identify the anatomical space into which drugs are injected during intrathecal administration.

questions.q: A patient with cryptococcal meningitis requires amphotericin B to achieve high cerebrospinal fluid concentrations rapidly because the drug poorly crosses the blood-brain barrier. Which route bypasses this barrier directly?
questions.explain: Intrathecal administration introduces medication directly into the subarachnoid CSF, overcoming poor penetration across the blood-brain barrier.

open.q: Which route of administration delivers drugs directly into the cerebrospinal fluid to bypass the blood-brain barrier?

questions.q: Which specialized route is used primarily for administering cytotoxic chemotherapy directly into the blood supply of a localized tumour or contrast media for angiography?
questions.explain: Intra-arterial injection delivers high local concentrations of anticancer drugs or radiopaque contrast directly to the target organ or limb before systemic dilution.

open.q: Name the vascular route used to deliver contrast media for angiography or regional chemotherapy directly to a target organ.

questions.q: Which route of administration is employed in emergency resuscitation of young children when peripheral intravenous access fails, allowing rapid fluid and drug infusion into the bone marrow cavity?
questions.explain: Intraosseous infusion (usually into the proximal tibia) accesses the non-collapsing medullary venous plexus, providing rapid systemic delivery equivalent to IV access.

open.q: Name the emergency route used to infuse fluids and drugs into the medullary cavity of a bone when IV access cannot be obtained.

questions.q: Why is the inhalational route particularly advantageous for administering salbutamol in bronchial asthma?
options: It delivers high local drug concentrations directly to bronchial smooth muscle with minimal systemic side effects
It guarantees 100% of the actuated dose reaches the alveoli
It converts salbutamol into an active metabolite in the nasal mucosa
It prolongs the drug half-life to 72 hours
questions.explain: Inhaled bronchodilators act directly on beta-2 receptors in the airways with rapid onset and low systemic plasma levels, reducing tremors and tachycardia.

open.q: Explain the therapeutic advantage of delivering salbutamol by inhalation rather than orally in asthma.
accept: high local airway concentration with fewer systemic side effects
rapid local bronchodilation and minimal systemic toxicity

questions.q: Which inhalational anesthetic property allows rapid induction and rapid recovery when administered via the lungs?
options: Large alveolar surface area and rapid gas exchange across the alveolar-capillary membrane
Active tubular secretion in the nephron
questions.explain: The huge surface area of the alveoli and thin alveolar-capillary membrane allow volatile anesthetics to equilibrate rapidly between alveolar air and arterial blood.

open.q: Why do volatile general anesthetics have a very rapid onset and offset of action when given by inhalation?
accept: large alveolar surface area and rapid diffusion across alveolar membrane
rapid gas exchange in the alveoli

questions.q: What physicochemical characteristic is required for a drug to be successfully delivered across intact skin using a transdermal therapeutic system (patch)?
options: Strong positive ionic charge at skin pH
High lipid solubility and high potency
questions.explain: To cross the lipid-rich stratum corneum at a clinically useful rate, transdermal drugs must be small, lipophilic, and potent enough that milligram-per-day doses suffice.

open.q: State two key physicochemical or pharmacological properties required for a drug to be formulated as a transdermal patch.
accept: high lipid solubility and high potency

questions.q: Which of the following clinical agents is commonly administered via a transdermal patch to provide steady plasma levels without first-pass metabolism?
questions.explain: Scopolamine (for motion sickness), fentanyl, nitroglycerin, nicotine, and estradiol are lipophilic, potent drugs delivered via transdermal patches.

open.q: Name an anticholinergic drug applied as a transdermal patch behind the ear to prevent motion sickness.

questions.q: Which route involves injecting a corticosteroid directly into a synovial cavity to treat localized osteoarthritis or rheumatoid synovitis?
questions.explain: Intra-articular injection places anti-inflammatory steroids (e.g., triamcinolone) directly inside the joint capsule, avoiding systemic steroid toxicity.

open.q: Name the route of administration used to inject drugs directly into a joint space.

questions.q: Why are sustained-release (controlled-release) oral tablets NOT suitable for crushing or chewing before swallowing?
options: Crushing inactivates the drug into toxic free radicals
Destroying the release matrix dumps the entire multi-hour dose at once, risking acute toxicity
Crushed tablets permanently stain dental enamel
The drug can only be absorbed in the oral cavity
questions.explain: Controlled-release formulations contain a large total dose designed to release slowly; crushing destroys the matrix and causes rapid dose-dumping and overdose.

open.q: Explain the danger of crushing or chewing a sustained-release oral tablet.
accept: rapid release of entire dose causing overdose

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of enteric-coating an oral tablet such as aspirin or omeprazole?
options: To increase drug absorption in the stomach
To mask the bitter taste in the mouth only
To prevent drug degradation by gastric acid or protect the gastric mucosa from irritation
To bypass hepatic portal blood flow completely
questions.explain: Enteric coatings resist dissolution in acidic gastric juice and dissolve only in the alkaline pH of the small intestine, protecting acid-labile drugs (omeprazole) or the stomach lining (aspirin).

open.q: State the two main clinical reasons for applying an enteric coating to oral tablets.
accept: protect drug from gastric acid and prevent stomach irritation
resist stomach acid and dissolve in intestine

questions.q: What type of parenteral preparation involves implanting a solid drug pellet or silastic capsule subcutaneously for prolonged hormone or contraceptive release over months to years?
questions.explain: Subcutaneous implants (such as levonorgestrel or etonogestrel implants) provide continuous, slow zero-order release of medication over extended periods.

open.q: Name the solid subcutaneous drug delivery form used for long-term contraception over several years.

questions.q: A 62-year-old man with severe nausea and persistent vomiting following abdominal surgery needs an antiemetic. Which route of administration is most appropriate?
questions.explain: In a patient with active vomiting, oral formulations will be expelled before absorption; parenteral (IV or IM) or rectal administration is indicated.

open.q: Which routes of administration are preferred over the oral route in a patient with persistent vomiting?

questions.q: An unconscious patient arrives at the accident and emergency department in hypoglycaemic coma. Why is the oral route strictly contraindicated in this patient?
options: Gastric absorption stops completely during coma
Loss of gag and swallowing reflexes creates a high risk of aspiration pneumonia
Oral administration triggers immediate cerebral oedema
questions.explain: Unconscious patients lack protective airway reflexes; administering fluids or tablets orally risks choking and fatal aspiration pneumonitis. Intravenous dextrose is required.

open.q: State the primary safety reason why oral medications and fluids are contraindicated in an unconscious patient.
accept: loss of gag reflex leading to aspiration

questions.q: How does the epidural route differ anatomically from the intrathecal route during regional analgesia?
options: Epidural injection enters the lateral ventricles of the brain
Epidural injection pierces the dura mater to mix directly with CSF
Epidural injection deposits the drug outside the dura mater without puncturing it
Epidural injection is administered into the peritoneal cavity
questions.explain: In epidural anaesthesia, local anesthetic is injected into the fat-filled epidural space outside the dura mater, avoiding dural puncture and post-dural puncture headache.

open.q: Explain the anatomical difference between epidural and intrathecal drug injection.
accept: epidural is outside the dura mater while intrathecal is inside the subarachnoid space
epidural does not pierce the dura mater

questions.q: Why is vasoconstrictor adrenaline (epinephrine) often co-administered with local anesthetics like lidocaine during subcutaneous infiltration?
options: To accelerate systemic clearance of lidocaine by the liver
To increase systemic toxicity and central nervous stimulation
To neutralize the acidic pH of the subcutaneous tissue
To produce local vasoconstriction that prolongs local anesthesia and reduces systemic absorption
questions.explain: Adrenaline stimulates alpha-1 receptors on local blood vessels, slowing systemic washout of lidocaine, prolonging nerve block duration, and lowering peak plasma toxicity.

open.q: Explain why adrenaline is added to local anesthetic injections during subcutaneous infiltration.
accept: causes vasoconstriction to prolong duration and reduce systemic absorption
slows systemic absorption and extends anesthesia

questions.q: Which local mucosal route is utilized when desmopressin or calcitonin is administered as a spray to achieve systemic effects?
questions.explain: The richly vascularized nasal mucosa allows rapid systemic absorption of peptide hormones like desmopressin and oxytocin without first-pass hepatic degradation.

open.q: Name the mucosal route used to administer systemic peptide sprays such as desmopressin.

questions.q: How can systemic side effects (such as bronchospasm from topical timolol eye drops) be minimized after instilling ophthalmic drops into the conjunctival sac?
options: By blinking rapidly 20 times immediately after instillation
By applying digital pressure over the medial canthus (nasolacrimal occlusion)
By rinsing the eye immediately with warm tap water
By instilling five drops simultaneously into each eye
questions.explain: Pressing on the medial canthus occludes the nasolacrimal duct, preventing drainage onto the highly vascular nasal mucosa where systemic absorption occurs without first-pass metabolism.

open.q: Describe the physical maneuver used after instilling eye drops to reduce systemic absorption through the nasolacrimal duct.

questions.q: What distinguishes a prodrug from an active drug?
options: A prodrug is excreted completely unchanged in the faeces
A prodrug is only used in veterinary medicine
A prodrug is pharmacologically inactive until converted into an active metabolite in vivo
A prodrug binds covalently and irreversibly to plasma albumin
questions.explain: Prodrugs (such as levodopa, enalapril, and clopidogrel) are inactive precursors designed to improve oral bioavailability, tissue penetration, or stability before enzymatic activation in the body.

open.q: Define a prodrug.
accept: inactive precursor converted to an active drug in the body
biologically inactive compound metabolized into an active drug

questions.q: Which of the following drugs is a monoclonal antibody produced by hybridoma or recombinant technology?
questions.explain: Monoclonal antibodies (ending in -mab, such as rituximab, trastuzumab, and infliximab) are biotechnology-derived biologics targeting specific antigens or receptors.

open.q: Give an example of a therapeutic monoclonal antibody produced via biotechnology.

questions.q: A hypertensive patient is prescribed oral propranolol, and the oral dose required is nearly ten times higher than the intravenous dose. Which phenomenon best explains this difference?
options: Complete failure of dissolution in gastric juice
questions.explain: Propranolol is well absorbed from the gut but undergoes heavy hepatic extraction during its first pass through the liver via the portal vein, requiring a much larger oral dose than IV dose.

open.q: Explain why the required oral dose of propranolol is vastly higher than its intravenous dose.

questions.q: Which parenteral route is used to administer depot antipsychotic formulations such as fluphenazine decanoate every 2 to 4 weeks?
questions.explain: Esterified depot antipsychotics dissolved in vegetable oil are injected deep intramuscularly to create a slow-release tissue reservoir lasting weeks.

open.q: Which route is used to administer oily depot antipsychotic injections for sustained action over weeks?

questions.q: What is a major disadvantage of the intravenous route compared to the oral route when an overdose or severe adverse reaction occurs?
options: The drug takes several hours to reach the systemic circulation
The drug cannot be retrieved or removed by gastric lavage or activated charcoal once injected
The drug undergoes complete inactivation by intestinal flora
questions.explain: Once an intravenous dose is administered, it is immediately in the systemic circulation and cannot be recalled, making strict asepsis and slow injection essential.

open.q: State a key safety disadvantage of intravenous administration compared with oral administration in the event of an overdose.
accept: drug cannot be retrieved once injected

questions.q: Which branch of pharmacology studies the beneficial and adverse effects of drugs in large human populations after clinical approval?
questions.explain: Pharmacoepidemiology applies epidemiological methods to study drug utilization, effectiveness, and safety across large real-world populations.

open.q: Name the discipline that studies the use and effects of drugs in large populations.
